question: Under N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, who is legally permitted to employ and supervise a New Jersey real estate salesperson?
choice_a: Any licensed salesperson with more than two years of experience
choice_b: The seller in a given transaction, directly
choice_c: Only a licensed New Jersey real estate broker
choice_d: A title insurance company handling the closing
explanation: N.J.S.A. 45:15-9 vests the authority to employ and supervise salespersons and broker-salespersons exclusively in licensed brokers; no other party may lawfully serve as a licensee's supervising employer.

question: A New Jersey broker-salesperson, despite being qualified to hold a full broker license, must still operate under what condition?
choice_a: No supervision at all, since broker-salespersons are treated as fully independent
choice_b: Supervision only by NJREC directly rather than by any broker
choice_c: Co-supervision shared equally between two different brokers
choice_d: Supervision by, and licensure under, an employing broker, the same as a standard salesperson
explanation: A broker-salesperson has met the qualifications to be a broker but has chosen to be licensed under, and work under the supervision of, another broker — functioning, for supervisory purposes, much like a salesperson.

question: A licensed salesperson wants to simultaneously accept assignments from two different unaffiliated brokers. Is this permitted under New Jersey law?
choice_a: No — a salesperson may be licensed under, and act for, only one employing broker at a time
choice_b: Yes, provided the salesperson discloses the arrangement to both brokers
choice_c: Yes, as long as the two brokers split the salesperson's license fee
choice_d: Yes, but only for rental transactions
explanation: A salesperson's license is tied to a single employing broker at any given time; New Jersey does not permit a salesperson to be simultaneously licensed under, or act on behalf of, more than one broker.

question: When a salesperson's employment with a broker ends, what must generally happen with respect to the salesperson's license?
choice_a: The salesperson may continue acting under the former broker's name until the license's next renewal date
choice_b: The salesperson must cease acting under the former broker's name and have the license transferred to, or reissued under, a new employing broker before resuming practice
choice_c: The salesperson automatically becomes an independent broker
choice_d: Nothing changes, since a salesperson's license is not tied to any particular broker
explanation: Because a salesperson's authority to practice flows from their employing broker, ending that employment relationship requires the salesperson to stop acting under the former broker and have their license reissued or transferred to a new employing broker before conducting further licensed activity.
source_note: hedge: general NJ salesperson-transfer practice consistent with N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: A broker's duty to supervise licensed salespersons in the office generally extends to which of the following?
choice_a: Only reviewing a salesperson's personal tax filings
choice_b: Only supervising transactions above a certain sale price
choice_c: Reviewing listing agreements, contracts, and advertisements prepared or used by salespersons in the office
choice_d: Nothing, since salespersons are solely responsible for their own compliance once licensed
explanation: An employing broker's supervisory responsibility includes oversight of the substantive work product of supervised salespersons — such as listing agreements, contracts, and advertising — because the broker bears ultimate responsibility for compliance in the office.
source_note: hedge: general NJ broker-supervision duty consistent with N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: Does classifying a New Jersey salesperson as an "independent contractor" for tax purposes change the licensing requirement that the salesperson operate under a supervising broker?
choice_a: Yes — independent contractor status eliminates the need for any supervising broker
choice_b: Yes — independent contractor status allows the salesperson to hold a broker license without additional education
choice_c: No — but only if the salesperson has fewer than three years of experience
choice_d: No — regardless of the tax classification used, a salesperson must still be licensed under and supervised by an employing broker
explanation: The independent contractor versus employee distinction relates to tax and compensation treatment, not to the licensing relationship; regardless of that classification, a salesperson must remain licensed under and supervised by a broker.

question: May a New Jersey broker directly employ and supervise another individual who is licensed as a broker-salesperson?
choice_a: Yes — a broker-salesperson, though qualified to be a broker, is licensed under and works for an employing broker just as a salesperson does
choice_b: No — a broker-salesperson cannot be supervised by anyone since they are already qualified as a broker
choice_c: No — a broker-salesperson may only be supervised by NJREC
choice_d: Yes, but only for a maximum of one year before the arrangement must end
explanation: A broker-salesperson holds broker-level qualifications but has elected to be licensed and practice under another broker's supervision, so an employing broker may lawfully employ and supervise a broker-salesperson the same way as a standard salesperson.

question: A buyer wants to pay a commission directly to the salesperson who represented them, bypassing the salesperson's broker. Is this permitted in New Jersey?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the buyer and salesperson put the arrangement in writing
choice_b: No — a salesperson may only be compensated for licensed activity by their own supervising broker, not directly by a client
choice_c: Yes, provided the amount is less than the broker's usual commission split
choice_d: Yes, if the salesperson has been licensed for more than five years
explanation: Because a salesperson's authority to earn commission flows through their employing broker, compensation for licensed real estate activity must be paid to the salesperson by that supervising broker, not directly by a client or third party.
source_note: hedge: general NJ commission-payment-channel rule consistent with N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: Broker A wants to pay a share of a commission directly to a salesperson who works for a different firm, Broker B, without routing the payment through Broker B. Is this permitted?
choice_a: Yes, as long as Broker A and the salesperson are personal friends
choice_b: Yes, provided the payment is under $500
choice_c: No — commission owed to a salesperson must be paid through that salesperson's own employing broker, not directly by another broker
choice_d: Yes, if the salesperson signs a waiver releasing Broker B from involvement
explanation: A salesperson may be compensated only through their own employing broker; even a cooperating broker on the other side of a transaction must pay commission owed to a salesperson by routing it through that salesperson's own broker.
source_note: hedge: general NJ commission-payment-channel rule consistent with N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: How is the amount of commission a New Jersey broker charges a client generally determined?
choice_a: It is fixed by NJREC regulation at a uniform statewide percentage
choice_b: It is set annually by the county board of realtors and binding on all members
choice_c: It is capped by statute at a flat dollar amount regardless of sale price
choice_d: It is negotiable between the broker and the client; New Jersey law does not set or fix commission rates
explanation: Real estate commission rates in New Jersey, as in other states, are a matter of negotiation and agreement between a broker and client; no state law or NJREC regulation fixes a mandatory commission rate.
source_note: hedge: general antitrust-consistent commission-negotiability principle, not pinpoint-cited

question: How is the split of a commission between a New Jersey broker and the salesperson who worked the deal generally determined?
choice_a: By the private compensation agreement between the broker and the salesperson, not by statute or NJREC regulation
choice_b: By a fixed 50/50 split mandated by the License Act
choice_c: By whatever percentage the buyer's attorney specifies at closing
choice_d: By NJREC on a per-transaction basis upon request
explanation: The internal division of commission between a broker and an affiliated salesperson is a matter of private contractual agreement between them; it is not dictated by the License Act or NJREC regulation.
source_note: hedge: general commission-split practice, not pinpoint-cited

question: When a broker receives a commission and owes a share of it to an affiliated salesperson, what is the broker generally expected to provide the salesperson?
choice_a: Nothing in writing, since verbal confirmation is always sufficient
choice_b: An accurate accounting or statement showing how the commission was calculated and disbursed
choice_c: A statement only if the salesperson formally demands one through NJREC
choice_d: A statement only once per calendar year covering all transactions
explanation: Sound recordkeeping and fair dealing practice require a broker to provide an accurate accounting of how a commission was calculated and disbursed whenever a salesperson is owed a share, consistent with the broker's overall accounting obligations.
source_note: hedge: general accounting/fair-dealing practice, not pinpoint-cited

question: At the closing of a real estate transaction, a New Jersey broker who handled trust monies is generally expected to provide clients with which of the following?
choice_a: Nothing, since disbursement details are confidential between the broker and the bank
choice_b: Only a verbal summary given at the closing table
choice_c: A settlement or accounting statement detailing how funds held on the client's behalf were disbursed
choice_d: A statement only if the client is a first-time buyer
explanation: Consistent with a broker's duty to account for funds handled on a client's behalf, a broker is expected to provide a settlement or accounting statement showing how any trust monies were ultimately disbursed.
source_note: hedge: general accounting-to-clients practice consistent with NJ trust-fund rules, not pinpoint-cited

question: A New Jersey broker is generally required to maintain accurate accounting records for which of the following?
choice_a: Only funds exceeding $50,000 in a single transaction
choice_b: Only commercial transactions, not residential ones
choice_c: Only funds that remain unclaimed for more than one year
choice_d: All money received on behalf of others in connection with real estate transactions
explanation: A broker's recordkeeping obligation covers all monies received on behalf of others in connection with real estate transactions, regardless of the dollar amount or property type, so that funds can always be accurately traced.
source_note: hedge: general NJ broker accounting/recordkeeping duty, not pinpoint-cited

question: If a party to a transaction requests a copy of an executed agreement the broker prepared or facilitated, what is the broker generally expected to do?
choice_a: Furnish a copy of the executed agreement to the requesting party
choice_b: Refuse, since executed agreements are considered the broker's proprietary property
choice_c: Charge a mandatory retrieval fee before releasing any copy
choice_d: Provide only a verbal summary of the agreement's terms
explanation: A broker is generally expected to furnish parties to a transaction with copies of executed agreements they signed, consistent with the broker's duty of fair dealing and proper recordkeeping.
source_note: hedge: general NJ recordkeeping/fair-dealing practice, not pinpoint-cited

question: A broker's financial and transaction records are subject to which of the following?
choice_a: Review only by the broker's own private accountant, with NJREC having no access
choice_b: Examination or audit by NJREC as part of its regulatory oversight
choice_c: Review only if a criminal indictment has already been filed
choice_d: No review of any kind once a transaction has closed
explanation: As the regulatory body overseeing real estate licensees, NJREC has authority to examine or audit a broker's financial and transaction records to verify compliance with the License Act and its regulations.
source_note: hedge: general NJREC audit/examination authority, not pinpoint-cited

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1, within how many business days of receipt must a New Jersey licensee deposit deposit/trust monies received in connection with a transaction into a special trust or escrow account?
choice_a: 24 hours
choice_b: 10 business days
choice_c: 5 business days
choice_d: 30 calendar days
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1 requires a licensee to deposit deposit or trust monies received in connection with a real estate transaction into a special trust/escrow account within five business days of receipt.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1, may a broker deposit a buyer's earnest money deposit into the same account the brokerage uses for its own operating expenses?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the broker keeps a mental note of which funds belong to whom
choice_b: Yes, provided the amount is under $1,000
choice_c: Yes, if the buyer gives verbal permission
choice_d: No — trust monies must be kept in a special account separate from the broker's own operating or personal funds, and may not be commingled
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1 specifically prohibits commingling client trust funds with a broker's own operating funds, requiring a dedicated special account for monies belonging to others.

question: Where must a New Jersey broker's trust or escrow account be maintained?
choice_a: In a banking institution authorized to do business in New Jersey, in an account designated for holding funds of others
choice_b: In the broker's personal safe, so the funds are always accessible
choice_c: In an out-of-state account chosen solely for the broker's convenience
choice_d: In a cryptocurrency wallet controlled by the broker
explanation: Trust or escrow funds must be held in a properly designated special account at a banking institution authorized to do business in New Jersey, ensuring the funds are traceable and protected from misuse.

question: A broker is short on operating cash and considers temporarily withdrawing funds from the brokerage's trust account to cover payroll, intending to replace the money once a commission check arrives. Is this permitted?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the broker repays the trust account within 5 business days
choice_b: No — using trust account funds for any purpose other than the purpose for which they were deposited is prohibited, even temporarily and even if the broker intends to repay it
choice_c: Yes, provided the withdrawal is documented in the broker's personal notes
choice_d: Yes, if the amount withdrawn is less than the broker's expected commission
explanation: Trust account funds belong to the parties on whose behalf they are held, not to the broker; using them for any other purpose — even temporarily with intent to repay — is a serious violation of trust account rules and a common basis for license suspension or revocation.

question: A buyer and seller both submit competing, conflicting demands for release of an earnest money deposit held in a broker's trust account after a contract dispute arises. What must the broker generally do?
choice_a: Release the funds immediately to whichever party contacts the broker first
choice_b: Release the funds to the seller automatically, since the seller is the broker's client
choice_c: Continue holding the disputed funds in the trust account and refrain from unilaterally releasing them to either party absent a mutual release, court order, or applicable dispute-resolution procedure
choice_d: Keep the funds permanently as the broker's own property since the deal fell apart
explanation: When there is a bona fide dispute over entitlement to escrowed funds, a broker must continue holding the money in trust and may not unilaterally disburse it to either party without a mutual written release, court order, or other lawful resolution procedure.
source_note: hedge: general escrow-dispute handling practice consistent with N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: A New Jersey brokerage's trust/escrow bank account should generally be titled or labeled in a way that does what?
choice_a: Uses only the broker's personal name with no other designation
choice_b: Uses a generic business name with no reference to trust or escrow funds at all
choice_c: Is left unlabeled to protect client confidentiality
choice_d: Clearly identifies it as a trust or escrow account holding funds belonging to others, distinguishing it from the broker's operating account
explanation: A proper trust or escrow account should be clearly designated as such so that the funds are unmistakably identified as belonging to others rather than to the broker, supporting the no-commingling requirement.

question: Why is regular reconciliation of a broker's trust account (comparing bank statements to the broker's internal ledger) an important compliance practice?
choice_a: It allows the broker to promptly detect shortages, errors, or unauthorized withdrawals before they become larger problems
choice_b: It is required only once, at the time the account is first opened
choice_c: It has no compliance value and is purely optional bookkeeping
choice_d: It is only necessary if the broker suspects a specific salesperson of wrongdoing
explanation: Regular reconciliation of the trust account against bank records is a key internal control that allows a broker to catch shortages, bookkeeping errors, or unauthorized withdrawals early, before they compound into larger regulatory or financial problems.
source_note: hedge: general trust-account internal-control best practice, not pinpoint-cited

question: New Jersey trust account recordkeeping requirements generally call for records to show which of the following for each deposit and disbursement?
choice_a: Only the total dollar amount currently in the account, with no transaction-level detail
choice_b: The identity of the parties involved, the property or transaction the funds relate to, and the applicable dates
choice_c: Only the broker's personal notes, without reference to any specific transaction
choice_d: Only the buyer's information, since the seller's identity is not relevant to escrow records
explanation: Proper escrow recordkeeping requires that each deposit and disbursement be traceable to the specific parties, property or transaction, and date involved, so that the trust account can be fully reconciled and audited.
source_note: hedge: general escrow-recordkeeping content requirement consistent with N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: New Jersey brokers are generally required to retain trust account and escrow transaction records for what purpose?
choice_a: For no defined period at all, since records may be discarded immediately after closing
choice_b: Only until the end of the calendar year in which the transaction closed, regardless of when it closed
choice_c: So that NJREC can review or audit them for a regulation-specified retention period following each transaction
choice_d: Only for transactions the broker personally handled, excluding those handled by supervised salespersons
explanation: Brokers must retain escrow and trust-related transaction records for a period specified by NJREC regulation so the records remain available for the Commission's review or audit, rather than being discarded shortly after closing.
source_note: hedge: general record-retention requirement consistent with N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1, not independently pinpoint-cited to an exact retention period

question: During a routine NJREC audit, an examiner asks to review a broker's escrow ledgers even though no complaint has been filed against the broker. Is NJREC permitted to do this?
choice_a: No — NJREC may only review records after a formal complaint has been filed
choice_b: No — trust account records are private and exempt from any regulatory review
choice_c: Yes, but only once every ten years
choice_d: Yes — NJREC has authority to examine a broker's trust account records as part of its regulatory oversight, independent of any specific complaint
explanation: NJREC's oversight authority includes the ability to examine or audit a broker's trust account records as part of routine regulatory supervision, not solely in response to a filed complaint.
source_note: hedge: general NJREC audit authority, not pinpoint-cited

question: A broker's escrow records show correct total balances but fail to identify which specific transaction each deposit and withdrawal relates to. Could this alone support NJREC disciplinary action?
choice_a: Yes — inadequate recordkeeping that fails to trace individual transactions can itself be a violation, even without any evidence that funds were actually misused
choice_b: No — as long as the total account balance is accurate, recordkeeping detail is irrelevant
choice_c: No — NJREC only disciplines brokers when client funds are actually stolen
choice_d: Yes, but only if the broker also fails to renew their license
explanation: Proper transaction-level recordkeeping is itself a regulatory requirement; failing to maintain records that trace each deposit and disbursement to a specific transaction can support discipline even absent proof that any funds were actually misapplied.
source_note: hedge: general escrow-recordkeeping compliance principle consistent with N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: A brokerage handles deposits for several different concurrent transactions in its trust account. What recordkeeping practice helps ensure each client's funds remain properly tracked?
choice_a: Recording all deposits and withdrawals from every transaction in a single undifferentiated line-item total
choice_b: Maintaining a separate ledger or subaccount record for each individual transaction's trust deposits within the overall trust account
choice_c: Relying solely on the bank's monthly statement with no internal ledger at all
choice_d: Keeping records only for the largest transaction handled that month
explanation: Maintaining a per-transaction ledger within the trust account allows a broker to track each client's funds individually, which is essential for accurate reconciliation and for demonstrating compliance if NJREC audits the account.
source_note: hedge: general escrow-recordkeeping best practice consistent with N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: If a salesperson working under a broker steals a client's deposit funds from the trust account without the broker's knowledge, who bears ultimate regulatory responsibility to NJREC for the trust account violation?
choice_a: No one, since the broker had no personal knowledge of the theft
choice_b: Only the salesperson, with the broker having no potential exposure of any kind
choice_c: The supervising broker, because a broker bears ultimate responsibility for the proper handling of trust funds in the office even when a salesperson working under them commits the actual misconduct
choice_d: The client, for failing to personally verify how their deposit was being held
explanation: Because trust accounts are maintained under the broker's license and supervisory authority, the broker bears ultimate responsibility to NJREC for their proper handling, even where a salesperson working under the broker is the one who actually misappropriated the funds.
source_note: hedge: general broker ultimate-responsibility principle consistent with N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1 and N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: Can a broker avoid responsibility for trust account violations by delegating day-to-day bookkeeping duties to an office manager or bookkeeper who is not a licensee?
choice_a: Yes — once delegated, responsibility shifts entirely to the office manager
choice_b: Yes, as long as the office manager signs a written indemnification agreement
choice_c: Yes, but only if the office manager has a college degree in accounting
choice_d: No — delegating bookkeeping tasks does not relieve the broker of ultimate legal responsibility for trust account compliance
explanation: A broker may delegate clerical or bookkeeping tasks, but the underlying legal responsibility for trust account compliance remains with the licensed broker and cannot be shifted to an unlicensed staff member through delegation alone.
source_note: hedge: general broker ultimate-responsibility principle, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: A salesperson personally receives a buyer's earnest money deposit check at the time a contract is signed. What should the salesperson do with the check?
choice_a: Promptly deliver the check to the supervising broker so it can be deposited into the trust account within the required deadline
choice_b: Hold onto the check personally until the closing date
choice_c: Deposit the check into the salesperson's own personal bank account for safekeeping
choice_d: Cash the check and hold the proceeds in a personal safe
explanation: Because the deposit deadline and trust account obligations run to the broker, a salesperson who personally receives client trust funds must promptly turn them over to the supervising broker so the funds can be timely and properly deposited.
source_note: hedge: general practice implementing the N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1 deposit deadline, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: Can NJREC take disciplinary action against a broker of record for trust account violations committed by a salesperson under that broker's supervision, even if the broker did not personally participate in the wrongdoing?
choice_a: No — NJREC's authority is limited strictly to the individual who personally committed the violation
choice_b: Yes — NJREC may hold a broker accountable for failures of supervision over trust funds in the office, given the broker's ultimate responsibility for the trust account
choice_c: No — a broker can only be disciplined for personal transactions in which they served as a party
choice_d: Yes, but only if the broker has been previously disciplined for an unrelated matter
explanation: Because the trust account operates under the broker's license and supervisory authority, NJREC can pursue disciplinary action against the broker of record for supervisory failures relating to trust fund handling, even where the broker did not personally commit the underlying misconduct.
source_note: hedge: general broker ultimate-responsibility and supervisory-liability principle, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: A broker collects a security deposit on a rental property they manage for a landlord client. Does the N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1 special-account and no-commingling requirement apply to this money?
choice_a: No — the trust account rule applies only to sale transactions, never to rental or property management funds
choice_b: No — security deposits are exempt from any special handling requirements
choice_c: Yes — trust account rules apply broadly to deposit and trust monies a licensee receives in connection with real estate transactions, which includes property management security deposits handled by a broker
choice_d: Yes, but only if the tenant specifically requests a separate account
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-5.1's special-account and no-commingling requirements apply broadly to funds of others received by a licensee in connection with real estate business, which includes security deposits and other monies a broker holds while managing rental property.

question: A broker discovers a bookkeeping error that has caused a temporary shortage in the trust account, unrelated to any theft. What is the broker's appropriate first step?
choice_a: Ignore the shortage as long as it resolves itself before the next NJREC audit
choice_b: Transfer money from a different client's trust funds to cover the shortfall without documenting the transfer
choice_c: Wait until year-end to address any trust account discrepancies
choice_d: Promptly correct the shortage by depositing sufficient funds to restore the account to the required balance and correct the underlying error
explanation: A broker who discovers a trust account shortage — even one caused by an honest bookkeeping error rather than misconduct — should promptly correct it and restore the required balance, since maintaining full trust funds at all times is a core compliance obligation.
source_note: hedge: general trust-account remediation best practice, not pinpoint-cited

question: Which of the following best describes the overall purpose of New Jersey's trust account and escrow recordkeeping requirements?
choice_a: To protect consumers' funds from misuse and ensure they can be accurately traced and returned or disbursed as intended
choice_b: To generate additional interest income for the broker personally
choice_c: To simplify the broker's own tax preparation at year-end
choice_d: To give NJREC a reason to collect additional licensing fees
explanation: Trust account and recordkeeping rules exist primarily to safeguard consumer funds held by licensees and ensure those funds are accurately tracked and properly applied or returned, protecting the public from mishandling or misappropriation.
source_note: hedge: general policy rationale for trust-account rules, not pinpoint-cited

question: A cooperating broker on the other side of a transaction offers a salesperson (not their own employee) a personal cash bonus for steering a buyer to a particular listing, paid directly to the salesperson rather than through the salesperson's own broker. Is this consistent with New Jersey's commission-payment-channel rules?
choice_a: Yes, since any broker may pay any salesperson directly as long as both agree
choice_b: No — compensation for licensed real estate activity must flow through the salesperson's own employing broker, not be paid directly to the salesperson by another broker
choice_c: Yes, provided the payment is disclosed to the buyer after closing
choice_d: Yes, if the amount is below the salesperson's usual commission split
explanation: Because a salesperson may only be compensated for licensed activity through their own employing broker, a direct side payment from another broker to the salesperson — bypassing the salesperson's broker — is inconsistent with New Jersey's commission-payment-channel requirements.
source_note: hedge: general NJ commission-payment-channel rule consistent with N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: Two brokers on opposite sides of a closed transaction agree to split the total commission according to their cooperating-broker agreement. How should each broker then pay the salesperson who represented their respective side?
choice_a: Both brokers must pay both salespersons equally regardless of which side each salesperson represented
choice_b: The salespersons must negotiate and collect their shares directly from the other side's broker
choice_c: Each broker pays their own affiliated salesperson out of the broker's own share, according to that broker's internal compensation agreement with the salesperson
choice_d: NJREC disburses the commission directly to each salesperson from a state fund
explanation: After brokers split a commission under their cooperating-broker agreement, each broker separately compensates their own affiliated salesperson out of that broker's share, consistent with the requirement that a salesperson be paid only through their own employing broker.
source_note: hedge: general two-broker commission-disbursement practice consistent with N.J.S.A. 45:15-9, not independently pinpoint-cited

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(a), when must a broker and a salesperson or referral agent enter into and sign a written business relationship agreement?
choice_a: Only if NJREC specifically requests one during an audit
choice_b: Within one year of the salesperson's initial licensure, regardless of when they actually started working
choice_c: Only if the salesperson expects to earn more than $5,000 in commissions that year
choice_d: Before the salesperson or referral agent engages in any real estate brokerage activity on the broker's behalf
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(a) requires that, prior to a salesperson or referral agent engaging in any real estate brokerage activity, the broker and the salesperson or referral agent must enter into and sign a written agreement containing the terms of their business relationship.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(a)2, absent a different payment schedule set out in the written agreement, within how many business days of the broker's receipt of commission funds (or as soon as those funds clear the broker's bank) must the broker pay the salesperson's or referral agent's earned portion?
choice_a: 10 business days
choice_b: 3 business days
choice_c: 15 calendar days
choice_d: 60 calendar days
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(a)2 requires the written agreement to include the broker's promise to pay the salesperson's or referral agent's portion of earned commissions within 10 business days of the broker's receipt of the funds (or as soon thereafter as the funds clear the broker's bank), unless another payment schedule is explicitly set forth in the agreement.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(d), what must a broker do if money due a salesperson or referral agent under their written agreement is not paid within 10 business days of the broker's receipt of the funds?
choice_a: Nothing, since the 10-day period is merely an aspirational guideline with no follow-up obligation
choice_b: Provide the salesperson or referral agent a complete written explanation of the failure to pay
choice_c: Automatically forfeit the entire commission to the salesperson as a penalty
choice_d: Report the delay to NJREC within 24 hours regardless of the reason for it
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(d) requires that if monies due a salesperson or referral agent are not paid within 10 business days of the broker's receipt (or promptly after the funds clear), the broker must provide the salesperson or referral agent a complete written explanation of the failure to pay.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(e), when a salesperson's or referral agent's affiliation with a broker ends, what must the broker provide, and by when?
choice_a: Nothing, since post-termination compensation is solely a matter between the salesperson and their new broker
choice_b: A verbal summary only, delivered at the moment of termination
choice_c: A complete written accounting of all monies due the salesperson or referral agent as of termination, and any that may become due in the future, within 30 days of the termination
choice_d: A written accounting, but only if the salesperson formally requests one in writing
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(e) requires that, within 30 days of the termination of a salesperson's or referral agent's affiliation with a broker, the broker must provide a complete written accounting of all monies due as of the date of termination and/or that may become due in the future.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(e), if the sums a broker accounts for after a salesperson's termination do not match the post-termination compensation terms of their written agreement, what must the broker also do?
choice_a: Simply pay whichever lower figure is more convenient, with no explanation required
choice_b: Refer the discrepancy to the salesperson's new broker to sort out
choice_c: Wait for NJREC to independently calculate the correct amount before responding
choice_d: Provide the salesperson or referral agent a written explanation of the difference along with the accounting
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(e) requires that if amounts accounted for after termination are not in accord with the post-termination compensation clause of the written agreement, the broker must give the salesperson or referral agent a complete written explanation of the difference along with the accounting.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(f), for how long must a broker maintain copies of licensee business relationship agreements, written explanations of late commission payments, and post-termination accountings, together with proof they were delivered to the salesperson or referral agent?
choice_a: Six years
choice_b: One year
choice_c: Three years
choice_d: Indefinitely, with no fixed minimum retention period
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(f) requires a broker to maintain copies of the business relationship agreement, any written explanations of late payment, and any post-termination accountings and explanations, along with proof of delivery to the salesperson or referral agent, for six years.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(g), if NJREC confirms that a broker has complied with this section's written-agreement and commission-payment requirements, what is the Commission's stated practice regarding a complaint alleging non-payment of a commission?
choice_a: The Commission will still conduct a full investigation regardless of the broker's demonstrated compliance
choice_b: The Commission will not further investigate the complaint unless it is accompanied by a copy of an arbitration decision (or equivalent) or a court judgment obtained by the salesperson or referral agent against the broker
choice_c: The Commission will automatically dismiss the complaint with no further recourse available to the salesperson
choice_d: The Commission will refer the matter directly to criminal prosecutors without further review
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(g) provides that if the Commission confirms a broker has complied with the section's requirements, it will not further investigate a non-payment-of-commission complaint unless the complaint is accompanied by a copy of an arbitration decision or the equivalent, or a court judgment the salesperson or referral agent secured against the broker.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(g), what happens if a broker fails to pay a salesperson or referral agent monies awarded by an unappealed arbitration decision or court judgment within 30 days of its effective date?
choice_a: Nothing further occurs; the salesperson must independently pursue collection with no regulatory involvement
choice_b: The salesperson's own license is automatically suspended instead of any action against the broker
choice_c: The broker becomes subject to sanctions under N.J.S.A. 45:15-17
choice_d: The underlying judgment or arbitration decision is automatically voided after 30 days
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(g) provides that, unless appealed, a broker's failure to pay monies awarded under an arbitration decision or judgment within 30 days of its effective date subjects the broker to sanctions pursuant to N.J.S.A. 45:15-17.

question: Do N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1's written-agreement and commission-accounting requirements apply only to salespersons, or also to real estate referral agents?
choice_a: They apply only to salespersons, never to referral agents
choice_b: They apply only to referral agents, since salespersons are covered exclusively by a separate, unrelated statute
choice_c: They apply to a referral agent only if that referral agent is also independently licensed as a broker-salesperson
choice_d: They apply equally to salespersons and to real estate referral agents
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1 expressly covers both salespersons and referral agents, requiring the same written business relationship agreement and commission-accounting protections for each.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(j), how does the New Jersey Real Estate Commission interpret references to "employment agreement," "employ," and "employing broker" found in N.J.S.A. 45:15-1 et seq. and this section?
choice_a: As permitting either an employment relationship or an independent contractor relationship between a broker and a broker-salesperson, salesperson, or referral agent
choice_b: As requiring every affiliated licensee to be treated strictly as a W-2 employee
choice_c: As prohibiting any independent contractor arrangement anywhere in New Jersey real estate practice
choice_d: As applying only to full-time salespersons, excluding any part-time licensees
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(j) clarifies that the Commission interprets "employment agreement," "employ," and "employing broker" to permit either an employment relationship or an independent contractor relationship between a broker and a broker-salesperson, salesperson, or referral agent.

question: Under N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(i), how broadly is the section's reference to "non-payment of a commission" construed?
choice_a: It applies only to commissions earned on residential sales, excluding rentals or referrals
choice_b: It is construed to include the non-payment of other forms of compensation, not just traditional sales commissions
choice_c: It applies only when the unpaid amount exceeds $10,000
choice_d: It excludes referral fees from its coverage entirely
explanation: N.J.A.C. 11:5-4.1(i) states that references to "non-payment of a commission" in the section are construed to include the non-payment of other forms of compensation, broadening the rule's reach beyond commissions in the narrowest sense.
